title: A Waterfall of Stars
caption: The galaxy UGCA 193, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: UGCA 193 · constellation Sextans · about z=0.002 (redshift) away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #97 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Looking rather like a waterfall, this galaxy seems to hold many young stars, especially in its lower part, which gives it a blue haze and the impression that stars are tumbling down from above. It is UGCA 193, a galaxy in the constellation Sextans, the Sextant, photographed by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.
That blue color tells us the stars on view are hot, some with temperatures more than 6 times the Sun's. To our eyes, cooler stars look redder and hotter stars look bluer.

A star's mass, surface temperature and color are all linked. Heavier stars burn at higher temperatures, so their surfaces glow blue. Massive blue stars also use up their fuel relatively quickly, which is why a strong blue glow like this one generally points to a population of young stars, recently formed in the galaxy.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed in visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published, though the caption links the blue haze to hot young stars.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye.
